title: I Gave AI Agents 3.5 Days to Build My Unreal Engine Game | Unreal's MegaJam Game Jam Devlog
author: KovatiDev
selftext:
I entered my first game jam, the Epic AI MegaJam 2026, with one laptop, AI agents, and a set of Unreal tools I’ve been building.

In 3.5 days we made Colony: Filed at Dawn, a third-person sci-fi detective mystery with no combat. You question the crew of a station, read records, drive through the rain, and drain flooded lower levels to reach an archive.

The clip shows some of the result. It’s an early alpha jam build, with plenty of rough edges.

A few things from the process:

* Agents sometimes sat idle while I thought work was progressing.
* Choosing the wrong environment kit created work that needed correcting later.
* Nine generated voices didn’t help when the scene was running at seven frames a second.
* I rejected a room and a wardrobe, and the opening cinematic went through five versions.
* The first real playthrough still uncovered problems close to the deadline.

I was directing, reviewing, testing, and explaining throughout. This also wasn’t a clean-room experiment: I brought existing Automation Forge tools, workflows, and third-party systems into the jam. The game uses Unreal Engine 5.8, Narrative Pro, and MetaHumans.

I recorded a devlog covering the process from the first terrain to the upload, including the failures.

For anyone else experimenting with agents in Unreal: what has been hardest to make reliable—getting them to understand the task, judging their output, or having them test it properly?

comments.author: ArtificialBeingsInc
comments.body:
Testing is the piece I’d separate from ‘the agent says done.’ Once there’s a playable slice, try a short path: question one crew member, read one record, and log frame time in the scene that was struggling. That gives you a playable checkpoint, not just a finished-task report.



For the idle agents, a visible ‘last activity / waiting on’ status could make a stall easier to spot, though silence alone doesn’t mean a task is stuck. Were yours waiting for input, or did they still appear to be working?
